Saba’s Industrials Intel
Our view: In this note we highlight key takeaways from the RBC Canadian Industrials Conference.
Key takeaways from RBC Capital Markets Canadian Industrials Conference
Last week (May 19-21), we hosted our annual RBC Canadian Industrials Conference in Toronto with 38
participating companies. From our coverage, companies in attendance included, Waste sector: WCN
(see note here). E&C: ARE (see note here), ATRL (see note here), STN (see note here), WSP (see note
here). Dealers: TIH (see note here). Auto/related: RBA (see note here), BYD/BGSI (see note here). Below
we note key takeaways from the event for our covered companies.

we note key takeaways from the event for our covered companies.
• Waste – Management commentary during calendar Q1 reporting and from the conference indicated
that the operating backdrop has directionally improved as the year has progressed, and companies
are well positioned relative to the initial guidance metrics (good likelihood of upward revisions to
guidance beginning with Q2/26 reporting, in our view). For WCN specifically, management expects
fuel surcharges to begin going into effect for the ~55% unhedged exposure in Q2 (100% recovery
expected in Q3 onward). As a second derivative impact, the higher oil price environment could also

benefit WCN's E&P business. Interestingly, the company expects ~100 bps of margin upside over the
coming years driven by AI-driven tools/initiatives.
• E&C – Commentary from the group indicated that the demand environment should get better as 2026
progresses. This view reflected increasing volume of nation-building initiatives in Canada, visibility to
a continuation of infrastructure investment in the U.S. via the proposed BUILD America 250 Act (aka
Surface Transportation Reauthorization), and stabilization of trends in APAC. With that said, AI-related
concerns continue to weigh on share prices/valuation across our global engineering coverage, with

most investor questions centered on when the focus may shift from AI risks, and what the market
needs to see in order to believe that further development of AI tools/capabilities is not a meaningful
risk to the group. In our view, investors are looking for these firms to deliver organic growth and margin
progression for a period of time while leveraging these tools, and more immediately, improved organic
growth over the course of 2026 should also help (we received some pushback around calendar Q1
reporting on headline organic growth across the group). While capital allocation has historically been

focused on M&A for the engineering group, investors have increasingly brought up return of capital
during recent discussions (with valuations lower across the group, investors are looking for increased
share buyback activity).
• Dealers – The outlook for infrastructure was generally in line with what we heard from the E&C
space (visibility improving given the nation-building initiatives), while TIH is starting to see Product
Support demand from fleet deliveries completed 2-3 years ago, with demand expected to ramp over
the coming years. The company is continuing to invest in the rental fleet ahead of anticipated demand,

noting bigger projects typically start with increased demand for rental equipment. On AVL, demand
remains robust (industry lead times go out into late-2027/2028; notably, the majority of Toromont's
backlog is expected to be delivered in the NTM), with the business primarily serving data centre
customers.
• Auto aftermarket/salvage – RBA management highlighted that the long-term secular trend of rising
loss rates/increasing cost of repair remain intact. Vehicle complexity also continues to increase, which
causes collision repair costs to rise and improves the appeal/economics of choosing the salvage

option, all else equal. On the CC&T business, management noted improved YoY customer sentiment
as Q1/H1 of last year were impacted by DOGE/tariff-related uncertainty. BYD management reiterated
that the long-term +3-5% SSS growth algorithm laid out in the company's 5-year plan remains intact,
where the ~2% annual headwind to volumes from ADAS is expected to be more than offset by an
increase in miles travelled/the number of vehicles on the road, increasing vehicle complexity, and
general inflation.
